# Delivery on Codex and ChatGPT

The planning workflow uses packaged skills, templates, reviewer lenses and tools
the current host actually exposes. It requires no delivery server or MCP
connection. Loading a planning skill alone does not launch persistent roles or
provide execution authority. The separately configured [local team runtime](team-runtime.md)
adds durable native roles, controlled artifact/Beads operations and explicit
operator acceptance. It does not merge, push or deploy. Project instructions and
permissions apply; an invoked skill does not grant unrelated authority.

## Establish available capabilities

Before each phase, identify the actual accessible project/artifacts, read and
write tools, shell/Python availability, search tools and authorized delegation.
Use available capabilities; do not assume them from a product name. Codex CLI,
Codex desktop, ChatGPT Chat and ChatGPT Work can expose different tools. Loading
a plugin cannot supply missing local filesystem access or install a service.

Resolve resources from the skill that the host loaded. From
`skills/<phase>/SKILL.md`, `../..` is this package's root when represented as files.
Use the host's resource reader when resources are exposed another way. A path
the host cannot open is unavailable, not permission to invent its contents.
Read the full active skill, its conventions and named inputs; after compaction,
read them again. References to "the user's request" mean actual conversation
context, not a literal argument variable. Use the host's skill picker; Codex
invocation examples use `$delivery:brief`, while ChatGPT can expose `@` selection.

## Artifacts and persistence

Choose one canonical artifact store for the initiative. In a local Codex project,
use its existing `.delivery/` and native file tools. With connected documents,
use only existing authorized read/write operations and preserve the same IDs,
initiative namespaces and history. Local file paths in phases are logical
artifact names in a document-backed workflow; they do not imply local access.

If the user provides uploaded files, treat them as identified snapshots. When
direct persistence is unavailable, return a complete document/export with its
intended filename, source revision and changes; say **prepared, not saved to the
canonical store**. A Markdown answer must not be reported as a repository update.
Do not silently establish a second canonical store. Missing source artifacts or
access keep their prerequisites unsatisfied; obtain the inputs instead of
fabricating current state. Status cannot infer a remote project's live state
from an old upload.

The Python helper is optional. Run it only with an actual shell, Python and
access to the selected workspace. Without those capabilities, inspect available
artifacts directly and label the result manual. For prose budgets, use an
available computation tool; if exact counting is unavailable, report the count
unverified instead of inventing a number. Never claim a command was run when
its result was inferred. Do not install an MCP server to make a planning phase
work.

## Review and coordination

Names such as `product-owner` identify documents in
`references/reviewers/<name>.md`, not registered tools or automatically running
team members. Read the applicable lens. Use native delegation only when exposed
and authorized by the project/session. Give reviewers the raw inputs and
read-only assignments without each other's findings; coordinate the result.

If delegation is unavailable or prohibited, use sequential passes labeled
**single-session review**. Do not call their agreement independent convergence.
Parallel-review steps and exit criteria are conditional on actual capability;
name missing independence in the handoff. A required independent release review
remains incomplete. Simulated personas always remain synthetic. Persistent
coordination uses the explicitly configured local runtime; assigning a role name
in a prompt alone does not create its durable native session.

## Evidence and authority

Separate source inspection, stub checks, real commands, real-model results and
UI observations. GUI claims need an inspected capture; CLI claims need actual
output and exit code; TUI layout needs a visual terminal capture. A sandbox test
does not establish behavior on an inaccessible customer host. Missing execution
or capture access means unable to check; prepare an explicit Codex/test handoff.

Planning `ready` is a manual assessment, not an enforced gate. Cite actual
decisions/evidence; do not invent `dec-`/`ev-` records, live role status or
authenticated consent. No plugin hooks or judge provider are enabled merely by loading a skill. The
[local runtime and judge commands](team-runtime.md) require explicit setup and a
real credentialed execution path on that surface. Judge selection is explicitly
disabled/Jev/OpenAI. Missing provider access never silently changes provider
or delegates the selected classification to host-model intuition. The host
model can still do ordinary planning without a separate judge. Neither model
classification nor a procedural phase check grants execution authority.
# Delivery conventions

Shared rules for the pipeline skills. A skill that points here is bound by every section
it names exactly as if that section were written in the skill itself. Read the whole file
once per skill run; it is short.

## Where `.delivery/` resolves to

Read `runtime.md` first. The filesystem rules below apply when local project
access actually exists. Otherwise `.delivery/...` names logical artifacts in the
explicit canonical document store or supplied snapshots. Preserve initiative
namespaces and IDs there. Return complete exports when writes are unavailable;
never claim local initialization or canonical persistence from a prepared draft.

Not necessarily the repository root. Resolve before reading or writing any artifact:

1. **Reuse.** Reuse the nearest existing ancestor `.delivery/`. If there is instead a nested component workspace, select that component explicitly; never create a second one beside it. The helper refuses ambiguity instead of picking a sibling.
2. **Explicit override.** Otherwise honor a delivery-root path stated in the nearest `AGENTS.md`.
3. **Ask, don't guess.** Otherwise, if this repository holds more than one independently-releasable component (multiple `package.json`/`plugin.json`/`pyproject.toml`, workspace members, or similar) stop and ask which component this work belongs to. Silently defaulting to the repo root in a multi-component repo is the failure this step exists to prevent.
4. **Default.** Otherwise, use `.delivery/` at the repository root.

## Which initiative

Every artifact below lives under `.delivery/initiatives/<slug>/`, never directly under
`.delivery/` — this is what lets independent initiatives (epics, sprints, parallel
workstreams) be planned in parallel branches without colliding on the same shared file
(`ADR-004`; the incident that motivated it: two initiatives independently continued the same
`S-n`/`FR-n` sequence in one shared `prd.md`, discovered only at merge). Resolve which
initiative before reading or writing any artifact:

1. **Explicit signal.** The user names an initiative, or one is already established for this
   conversation — use it.
2. **Exactly one exists.** If `.delivery/initiatives/` has exactly one subdirectory, use it
   without asking — this keeps single-initiative projects exactly as simple as before this
   convention existed.
3. **Ask, don't guess.** Otherwise (zero, or more than one, with no explicit signal) — ask
   which initiative this work belongs to, or whether to start a new one. Never silently
   default to the most recently modified one.
4. **Starting a new initiative.** Confirm its slug (kebab-case, derived from the brief
   subject or what the user names) before creating `.delivery/initiatives/<slug>/` — check it
   doesn't collide with an existing initiative slug or any other top-level `.delivery/` entry.
   A genuinely new initiative needs its own `$delivery:brief`, or an explicit
   `extends: <existing-slug>` note (in this new initiative's own first artifact) declaring it
   reuses an existing initiative's problem framing instead of running its own — state which,
   don't leave it implicit.

Cross-cutting, project-wide, never per-initiative: `.delivery/glossary.md`,
`.delivery/personas/`, `.delivery/interviews/`, `.delivery/simulations/`,
`.delivery/decisions/ADR-NNN-*.md`. This preview has no invocation ledger.
`.delivery/stories/`, `.delivery/reviews/`, `.delivery/sprints/` stay flat but are prefixed
by initiative slug, matching `stories/<slug>-NN-<name>.md`'s existing convention.

## Open blocking findings

Read `.delivery/reviews/`. If any finding against an artifact
this phase consumes has status `open` and severity `blocking`, **stop and report them** — do
not proceed. A blocking finding is one a reviewer said must be resolved before this point;
building on it means every downstream artifact inherits a known, documented defect with no
resolution on record.

Resolving means the finding is marked `fixed`, or `rejected` with the reason recorded. The
user may still choose to proceed over an open finding — that is their call, not a default.
Ask, and record what they chose.

## Language

Read `.delivery/glossary.md` first and use its terms exactly. If it does not exist, create
it as *Keeping the glossary* below says — or, for a small effort, collect terms as you go and
propose the file at the end. Do not coin synonyms for concepts it already names.

Any term you need that is missing gets **proposed explicitly**, with a definition in the
business's vocabulary and a concrete referent. Any term carrying two meanings gets raised as
a defect, not resolved silently.

**Questions go out in the vocabulary of whoever must answer them**, with a worked example in
their world. A question for the business owner written in engineering terms is a blocker
with a name on it, not a question. If a question is really an engineering call, decide it
here rather than routing it to them.

### Keeping the glossary

`.delivery/glossary.md`, one agreed term per concept, written from
`../templates/glossary.md` (budget: 500 words target, 900 hard cap). It is
project-wide and every skill reads it; any skill that coins or meets a new term adds it.
Every document is written by someone fluent in a different dialect — the analyst's *booking
window* is the architect's *date range* and the owner's *price list* — and the damage shows
at the edges: questions the owner cannot answer, requirements that drift into two concepts,
and a hand-off the runner has to guess at.

1. **Curate, never regenerate.** If the file exists, edit it. Terms are stable: changing a
   definition means saying what it was, what it is now, and which documents were written
   under the old meaning.
2. **Harvest the terms actually in use** — the originator's own words first (they outrank
   everything), then the brief, PRD, personas, architecture, and real identifiers in code
   and data.
3. **Resolve collisions.** Synonyms (several words, one concept): pick one, list the rest as
   *aliases, not to be used*, with the document each came from. Homonyms (one word, several
   concepts): split them and rename at least one.
4. **Let the business word win.** Where domain and code disagree, the domain term is the
   entry and the code identifier is recorded as its implementation name. Do not rename code
   as a side effect.
5. **Define in the owner's words**, plain sentence first, precise one after if needed, and
   **ground each term** in a worked example, a file path or a value from the data.
6. **A term nobody can define crisply** is an unresolved product decision wearing a noun:
   list it as an open question for the originator, never invent a definition.
7. **Sweep for completeness.** Every domain noun in the existing artifacts appears in the
   glossary or is deliberately excluded, and no synonym is left without one canonical term.

**Report what changed** when you hand off: new terms, resolved synonyms, and any term that could
not be defined. Those are product decisions, and they belong to the originator.

During `$delivery:status`, manually compare the active artifacts with the glossary; the inventory helper does not extract domain terms.

## Writing, then revising

The skill states the budget: a word target and a hard cap (both exclude code, YAML and data tables).

**Compose first. Do not try to hit the budget while writing.** Restraint during
composition trades substance for brevity in the wrong order — the findings get thinner
while the scaffolding survives. Write what the artifact needs, then cut what it does not.

**Then measure, do not estimate.** The budget counts **prose only**. Data tables, code
blocks and YAML are excluded, so measure with them stripped:

With local execution, use the helper below. On another surface, use available
computation tools with the same exclusions. If none are available, preserve the
substance and state **word count unverified**; an exact-count exit criterion
remains unverified. Do not invent a count or require a new server for counting.

```sh
python3 <resolved-plugin-root>/scripts/project.py words <artifact-path>
```

The helper strips HTML comments, initial YAML frontmatter, fenced code and
pipe-prefixed table rows before counting prose. Use pipe-prefixed data tables.
Inline code remains prose; this is a Markdown budget convention, not a full parser.

A plain `wc -w` counts the tables and will overstate the total, often by several times.
Measuring the wrong number leads to cutting the wrong thing.

**Rows in a data table can never help you meet the budget, because they are not counted.**
Deleting them is pure loss for zero benefit. The term table, the requirement table, the
findings table, the friction map — these *are* the artifact. If a revision pass is removing
rows, it has misunderstood the rule and should stop.

**If the count exceeds the hard cap, you are not finished.** Make a revision pass over the file and
delete, in this order, until it fits:

1. Preamble, recap, and any sentence describing what the document is about to say
2. **Restatement** — the same fact as prose *and* a table row *and* a summary bullet. Keep the form that carries it best; delete the others. This is almost always the biggest win.
3. Process narration — "I examined X and found Y" becomes Y
4. Hedging — either you know it, or it is labelled an assumption. Both are shorter.
5. Citations past the first for a given claim

# Product brief

Subject: **the user's request**

DEFINE stage, the entry point. Output: `.delivery/initiatives/<initiative>/brief.md`.

## Conventions

Read [host capability guidance](../../references/runtime.md) and
[delivery conventions](../../references/conventions.md) before running this phase.

## Pick the mode first, and say which

The two jobs are different sizes and different documents. State the mode in the brief's header.

| Mode | When | Budget |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| **Frame** | A new feature or product. The problem is ahead of you. | target 600 words, cap 900 |
| **Assess** | An existing, working product. The problems are already in the code. | target 1200 words, cap 2000 |

If the target is an existing codebase and the request is to evaluate it, that is **assess**.
A new capability for an existing product is **frame** — the existing product is context,
not the subject.

## Gate check

No prerequisites — this is the entry point. If `.delivery/initiatives/<initiative>/brief.md`
already exists, read it and ask whether to **revise**, **replace**, or **start new version**.
See `../../templates/version-history.md` for what each means, the
same-problem test that chooses between revise and start new version, and the
Version-history table and Corrections log it writes. Never silently overwrite.

## Run

**1. Understand the ground truth.** If a codebase exists, read it before writing anything
about what should be. Note the current behavior, and how you would verify a claim about it.

**2. Find, convergently — this is the part that determines whether the brief is any good.**

A single analytical pass finds *some* of what is there, not the most important of it. Two
passes over the same code, prompted the same way, return overlapping-but-different sets, and
the difference is not correlated with severity. Running once and reporting the result as
"the problems" overstates what one pass knows.

Use at least three different lenses. When native delegation is available and
authorized, give separate read-only reviewers the same raw inputs and keep their
findings separate until synthesis. Otherwise use sequential passes in this
session, labeled single-session review. Do not require unavailable delegation.

| Lens | Review lens | Asks |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Value | `product-owner` lens | Who has this problem, what does it cost them, what would success look like |
| Precision | `business-analyst` lens | What is ambiguous, what cases are unhandled, what numbers are missing |
| Absence | `feature-critic` lens | What is *not* here that should be — the unasked question, the missing state |

In **assess** mode add a fourth:

| Decay | `qa-strategist` lens | What was true when written and is not true now — dated data, expiring calendars, stale rates, assumptions with a shelf life |

That lens exists because temporal defects are invisible to structural review. A test suite
checks whether data has the right shape, never whether it is still true.

If independent reviewers are unavailable, use sequential lens passes and explicitly
label the result **single-session review**. Do not count agreement as independent convergence.

**3. Merge and report the actual review mode.** Deduplicate. For isolated native
reviewers, record how many found each issue independently. In single-session
mode, record which lens raised each issue but mark independent convergence
unavailable; repeated agreement is not independent evidence. Keep findings
raised by only one lens rather than hiding uncertainty.

Then state the coverage honestly: if each lens surfaced material the others did not, the
space is **not exhausted**, and the brief should say so rather than implying completeness.

**4. Verify before asserting.** Any finding with a number in it — a count, a price, a date —
gets checked against the source before it enters the brief. Specific, confident and wrong is
the worst thing this phase can produce, because precision reads as authority.

**5. Ask what you cannot determine.** Collect open questions, drop the ones the codebase
answers, put the rest to the user in one batch. Record what stays unanswered. Never invent
an answer, and never quietly drop a question because it is inconvenient.

**6. Write** to `.delivery/initiatives/<initiative>/brief.md` using `../../templates/brief.md`.

## Exit criteria

- Mode stated, and the document within that mode's cap — **or the overrun declared in the document with its reason**. Measure prose when computation is available; otherwise report word count unverified.
- Review mode stated, at least three lenses used, and independent convergence recorded only when reviewers were actually isolated
- Coverage stated: whether the finders agreed enough to call the space explored
- Every numeric claim verified against its source
- A named user segment, not "users"
- The problem stated as something happening today, with its cost
- At least one measurable success signal
- Explicit out-of-scope list
- Open questions with owners, where any remain

## Writing

Obey `../../templates/writing-standard.md`.

The budget above is a hard check, not an aspiration. Before finishing, measure prose excluding code, YAML and data tables with
an available computation tool. If none is available, state word count unverified;
do not invent a count or claim the budget check passed. Over the cap, cut restatement, process narration and
hedging — never findings, citations, grounding labels, open questions or IDs. If it still
does not fit, keep the substance and **write the overrun and its reason into the document**.
A declared overrun is a judgement; a silent one is a habit.

## Hand off

Report exit criteria status, the convergence picture, and anything found by only one lens.
If the finders disagreed enough that the space looks unexplored, say so — that is a reason
to run again, not to proceed.

Next step: `$delivery:challenge .delivery/initiatives/<initiative>/brief.md`, then `$delivery:research`.

The planning workflow uses packaged skills, templates, reviewer lenses and tools
the current host actually exposes. It requires no delivery server or MCP
connection. Loading a planning skill alone does not launch persistent roles or
provide execution authority. The separately configured [local team runtime](team-runtime.md)
adds durable native roles, controlled artifact/Beads operations and explicit
operator acceptance. It does not merge, push or deploy. Project instructions and
permissions apply; an invoked skill does not grant unrelated authority.

## Establish available capabilities

Before each phase, identify the actual accessible project/artifacts, read and
write tools, shell/Python availability, search tools and authorized delegation.
Use available capabilities; do not assume them from a product name. Codex CLI,
Codex desktop, ChatGPT Chat and ChatGPT Work can expose different tools. Loading
a plugin cannot supply missing local filesystem access or install a service.

Resolve resources from the skill that the host loaded. From
`skills/<phase>/SKILL.md`, `../..` is this package's root when represented as files.
Use the host's resource reader when resources are exposed another way. A path
the host cannot open is unavailable, not permission to invent its contents.
Read the full active skill, its conventions and named inputs; after compaction,
read them again. References to "the user's request" mean actual conversation
context, not a literal argument variable. Use the host's skill picker; Codex
invocation examples use `$delivery:brief`, while ChatGPT can expose `@` selection.

## Artifacts and persistence

Choose one canonical artifact store for the initiative. In a local Codex project,
use its existing `.delivery/` and native file tools. With connected documents,
use only existing authorized read/write operations and preserve the same IDs,
initiative namespaces and history. Local file paths in phases are logical
artifact names in a document-backed workflow; they do not imply local access.

If the user provides uploaded files, treat them as identified snapshots. When
direct persistence is unavailable, return a complete document/export with its
intended filename, source revision and changes; say **prepared, not saved to the
canonical store**. A Markdown answer must not be reported as a repository update.
Do not silently establish a second canonical store. Missing source artifacts or
access keep their prerequisites unsatisfied; obtain the inputs instead of
fabricating current state. Status cannot infer a remote project's live state
from an old upload.

The Python helper is optional. Run it only with an actual shell, Python and
access to the selected workspace. Without those capabilities, inspect available
artifacts directly and label the result manual. For prose budgets, use an
available computation tool; if exact counting is unavailable, report the count
unverified instead of inventing a number. Never claim a command was run when
its result was inferred. Do not install an MCP server to make a planning phase
work.

## Review and coordination

Names such as `product-owner` identify documents in
`references/reviewers/<name>.md`, not registered tools or automatically running
team members. Read the applicable lens. Use native delegation only when exposed
and authorized by the project/session. Give reviewers the raw inputs and
read-only assignments without each other's findings; coordinate the result.

If delegation is unavailable or prohibited, use sequential passes labeled
**single-session review**. Do not call their agreement independent convergence.
Parallel-review steps and exit criteria are conditional on actual capability;
name missing independence in the handoff. A required independent release review
remains incomplete. Simulated personas always remain synthetic. Persistent
coordination uses the explicitly configured local runtime; assigning a role name
in a prompt alone does not create its durable native session.

## Evidence and authority

Separate source inspection, stub checks, real commands, real-model results and
UI observations. GUI claims need an inspected capture; CLI claims need actual
output and exit code; TUI layout needs a visual terminal capture. A sandbox test
does not establish behavior on an inaccessible customer host. Missing execution
or capture access means unable to check; prepare an explicit Codex/test handoff.

Planning `ready` is a manual assessment, not an enforced gate. Cite actual
decisions/evidence; do not invent `dec-`/`ev-` records, live role status or
authenticated consent. No plugin hooks or judge provider are enabled merely by loading a skill. The
[local runtime and judge commands](team-runtime.md) require explicit setup and a
real credentialed execution path on that surface. Judge selection is explicitly
disabled/Jev/OpenAI. Missing provider access never silently changes provider
or delegates the selected classification to host-model intuition. The host
model can still do ordinary planning without a separate judge. Neither model
classification nor a procedural phase check grants execution authority.
# Delivery conventions

Shared rules for the pipeline skills. A skill that points here is bound by every section
it names exactly as if that section were written in the skill itself. Read the whole file
once per skill run; it is short.

## Where `.delivery/` resolves to

Read `runtime.md` first. The filesystem rules below apply when local project
access actually exists. Otherwise `.delivery/...` names logical artifacts in the
explicit canonical document store or supplied snapshots. Preserve initiative
namespaces and IDs there. Return complete exports when writes are unavailable;
never claim local initialization or canonical persistence from a prepared draft.

Not necessarily the repository root. Resolve before reading or writing any artifact:

1. **Reuse.** Reuse the nearest existing ancestor `.delivery/`. If there is instead a nested component workspace, select that component explicitly; never create a second one beside it. The helper refuses ambiguity instead of picking a sibling.
2. **Explicit override.** Otherwise honor a delivery-root path stated in the nearest `AGENTS.md`.
3. **Ask, don't guess.** Otherwise, if this repository holds more than one independently-releasable component (multiple `package.json`/`plugin.json`/`pyproject.toml`, workspace members, or similar) stop and ask which component this work belongs to. Silently defaulting to the repo root in a multi-component repo is the failure this step exists to prevent.
4. **Default.** Otherwise, use `.delivery/` at the repository root.

## Which initiative

Every artifact below lives under `.delivery/initiatives/<slug>/`, never directly under
`.delivery/` — this is what lets independent initiatives (epics, sprints, parallel
workstreams) be planned in parallel branches without colliding on the same shared file
(`ADR-004`; the incident that motivated it: two initiatives independently continued the same
`S-n`/`FR-n` sequence in one shared `prd.md`, discovered only at merge). Resolve which
initiative before reading or writing any artifact:

1. **Explicit signal.** The user names an initiative, or one is already established for this

2. **Exactly one exists.** If `.delivery/initiatives/` has exactly one subdirectory, use it

3. **Ask, don't guess.** Otherwise (zero, or more than one, with no explicit signal) — ask
   which initiative this work belongs to, or whether to start a new one. Never silently
   default to the most recently modified one.
4. **Starting a new initiative.** Confirm its slug (kebab-case, derived from the brief
   subject or what the user names) before creating `.delivery/initiatives/<slug>/` — check it
   doesn't collide with an existing initiative slug or any other top-level `.delivery/` entry.

   `extends: <existing-slug>` note (in this new initiative's own first artifact) declaring it
   reuses an existing initiative's problem framing instead of running its own — state which,
   don't leave it implicit.

Cross-cutting, project-wide, never per-initiative: `.delivery/glossary.md`,
`.delivery/personas/`, `.delivery/interviews/`, `.delivery/simulations/`,
`.delivery/decisions/ADR-NNN-*.md`. This preview has no invocation ledger.
`.delivery/stories/`, `.delivery/reviews/`, `.delivery/sprints/` stay flat but are prefixed
by initiative slug, matching `stories/<slug>-NN-<name>.md`'s existing convention.

## Open blocking findings

Read `.delivery/reviews/`. If any finding against an artifact
this phase consumes has status `open` and severity `blocking`, **stop and report them** — do
not proceed. A blocking finding is one a reviewer said must be resolved before this point;
building on it means every downstream artifact inherits a known, documented defect with no
resolution on record.

Resolving means the finding is marked `fixed`, or `rejected` with the reason recorded. The
user may still choose to proceed over an open finding — that is their call, not a default.
Ask, and record what they chose.

## Language

Read `.delivery/glossary.md` first and use its terms exactly. If it does not exist, create
it as *Keeping the glossary* below says — or, for a small effort, collect terms as you go and
propose the file at the end. Do not coin synonyms for concepts it already names.

Any term you need that is missing gets **proposed explicitly**, with a definition in the
business's vocabulary and a concrete referent. Any term carrying two meanings gets raised as
a defect, not resolved silently.

**Questions go out in the vocabulary of whoever must answer them**, with a worked example in
their world. A question for the business owner written in engineering terms is a blocker
with a name on it, not a question. If a question is really an engineering call, decide it
here rather than routing it to them.

### Keeping the glossary

`.delivery/glossary.md`, one agreed term per concept, written from
`../templates/glossary.md` (budget: 500 words target, 900 hard cap). It is
project-wide and every skill reads it; any skill that coins or meets a new term adds it.

window* is the architect's *date range* and the owner's *price list* — and the damage shows
at the edges: questions the owner cannot answer, requirements that drift into two concepts,

1. **Curate, never regenerate.** If the file exists, edit it. Terms are stable: changing a

7. **Sweep for completeness.** Every domain noun in the existing artifacts appears in the
   glossary or is deliberately excluded, and no synonym is left without one canonical term.

**Report what changed** when you hand off: new terms, resolved synonyms, and any term that could
not be defined. Those are product decisions, and they belong to the originator.

During `$delivery:status`, manually compare the active artifacts with the glossary; the inventory helper does not extract domain terms.

The skill states the budget: a word target and a hard cap (both exclude code, YAML and data tables).

composition trades substance for brevity in the wrong order — the findings get thinner

## The three choices

If a governed artifact already exists, read it and ask whether to **revise**, **replace**,

- **Revise** — the new scope is the same problem as the current version's own problem

- **Replace** — discard the current content entirely and start over on the same problem.

  `.delivery/glossary.md` and other documents for citations into this artifact first).
- **Start new version** — the new scope is a different problem than the current version's,

## Same-problem test

current version's own Problem section? If there is a genuine match against a document

reaction, proceed on the test's own output rather than blocking on silence.

| Document | Primary anchor | Universal anchor |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `brief.md` | `## Problem` | Scope cell |

## Version-history table

Added only when a document starts its own second version — never baked into a
first-version template. When a tableless document starts one, all prior content is
retroactively labelled `## Version 1` and the table is inserted before it, not after
(see the diff-check note below).

```
| Version | Date | Status | Scope |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | YYYY-MM-DD | in progress \| shipped \| shipped · debt open \| shipped · debt closed YYYY-MM-DD | ≤20 words / ≤140 chars, never blank |
```

**Status-cell vocabulary — closed set:** `in progress` \| `shipped` \| `shipped · debt
open` \| `shipped · debt closed <ISO date>`. Anything outside this set means the test is
unable to be applied — never guess which value was meant; report it and ask. Distinct
from, and never required to match, the document's separate header `Status:` line, which
stays freer prose.

**Scope cell:** ≤20 words / ≤140 characters, never blank. Measure before writing.

**Date cell:** ISO 8601 `YYYY-MM-DD`. Records the version's opening date only — a closing
date, if different from the opening date, goes in the Status cell text
(`shipped · debt closed <ISO date>`), not the Date cell.

**Row count:** no hard limit, but reconsider this lightweight table's approach once any
one document exceeds roughly 6 rows — flag it, don't block on it.

**Version numbers strictly increase — no gaps, no duplicates.** A correction found in a
closed version's row never renumbers it; the Corrections log annotates it instead, per
below.

**Staleness keys off the current version's own Date cell, not the file's mtime.** A file
can be touched (reformatted, a typo fixed) without a new version starting, so file
modification time alone over- and under-reports staleness. Compare downstream documents'
own current-version Date cells against this one's — an old file mtime with a recent
current-version Date cell is not stale; a recent mtime with an old current-version Date
cell may still be.

version N — an in-place edit of the not-yet-closed row's own Status cell, freely
permitted as routine progress. The row freezes only once that edit lands.

error gets a Corrections log entry instead, and the original row keeps its version

| Date noted | Corrects version | What was wrong | Correct value |

# Product brief: Tiny ASCII slugifier

> Written using delivery:brief. Owned by Product Manager.
> Status: draft · Last updated: 2026-10-20

**Mode:** frame · **Word count:** 433 (cap 900)

## Coverage

Single-session review using sequential value, precision and absence lenses. Independent convergence is unavailable. Each lens surfaced a distinct concern; the space is not exhausted. This draft frames only the bounded CLI contract.

| Lens | Ran | Distinct finding |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Value | Yes | Shell users need predictable text conversion; user demand and time savings are unverified. |
| Precision | Yes | Unicode-aware character classes or lowercasing could violate the ASCII-only contract. |
| Absence | Yes | Empty results and missing arguments need observable outcomes so scripts can distinguish them. |

Source: the supplied drafting request and existing `delivery-plan.md` in this initiative. Product inspection found only `README.md`, which describes the intended fixture; no CLI implementation was observed. No product tests have run. Hosted CI is not present.

## Problem

The fixture currently provides no executable text-to-slug command. A shell user needing a consistent ASCII label must supply their own conversion. Inconsistent handling of punctuation and Unicode can produce different labels for the same text.

The user need and workaround are product assumptions, not findings from interviews.

## Who has it

Developers and script authors working in a terminal who need a deterministic ASCII slug from a text argument. Audience size and usage frequency are unknown.

## Cost of the status quo

Assumed costs are repeated manual editing or ad hoc scripts, plus errors from differing separator rules. No time, financial cost or error-rate baseline has been collected.

## What changes if we solve it

A terminal user invokes `python3 slugify.py TEXT` in the product root and receives a predictable line suitable for capture by a shell script. For example, `" Hello, WORLD! "` becomes `hello-world` followed by a newline.

## Success signals

| Signal | How measured | Current | Target |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Contract correctness | Observe stdout and process exit status for ordinary text, separator runs, edge separators, Unicode, all-separator text and missing TEXT | Unverified; no execution evidence | Every specified behavior matches the story |
| Repeatability | Invoke the same text repeatedly and compare output | Unverified | Identical output |

## MVP boundary

Deliver `slugify.py` in product root `/private/var/folders/2r/5gvkx5wx0g37m4grvjjdt88m0000gn/T/delivery-full-cli-3b8pu1g_/product`.

Accept exactly one text argument. Lowercase ASCII A-Z, replace each maximal run outside ASCII [A-Za-z0-9] with a hyphen, trim edge hyphens, and print the result followed by a newline with exit 0. Unicode outside ASCII acts as a separator. All-separator text prints an empty line. Missing TEXT exits 2.

## Explicitly out of scope

- Transliteration, Unicode alphanumeric retention and locale-specific conversion.
- Batch processing, stdin input, file output and packaging.
- Collision avoidance, uniqueness guarantees and URL validation.
- Additional acceptance requirements for extra arguments or diagnostic wording.

## Current-state workflow

The observed product README asks for an ASCII-only terminal slugifier. The assumed current user workflow is to edit text manually or write a conversion script, then inspect its output. That workflow has not been observed with real users.

## Open questions

No blocking question remains for the specified contract.

| Question | Owner | Blocks |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| How often do terminal script authors need this conversion, and what errors occur today? | Product Manager | Value validation; does not block this fixture draft |

Proposed glossary term: **slug** means the resulting lowercase ASCII alphanumeric text with internal separator hyphens; for example, `hello-world`. No separate glossary artifact is created in this bounded drafting stage.

name: stories
description: "Decompose a roadmap phase into self-contained, implementation-ready story files that carry their full context. Use when a phase is about to start and the work needs to be broken into pickable units. Produces .delivery/stories/."
---

# Story decomposition

Phase or epic to decompose: **the user's request** (defaults to the first phase not yet decomposed)

CONTRACT stage. Inputs: `.delivery/initiatives/<initiative>/prd.md`, `.delivery/initiatives/<initiative>/architecture.md`, `.delivery/initiatives/<initiative>/roadmap.md`, plus `design-system.md` where it exists. Output: `.delivery/stories/`.

## Conventions

Read [host capability guidance](../../references/runtime.md) and
[delivery conventions](../../references/conventions.md) before running this phase.

## Gate check

Read all three inputs and list any existing stories in `.delivery/stories/`.

- **Roadmap missing** — stop and run `$delivery:roadmap` first. Without it there is no defensible phase boundary to decompose along.
- **Architecture missing** — warn hard. Stories written without a design either omit the technical context (making them un-pickable) or invent a design inline (which is the Solution Architect's job, done badly). Recommend running `$delivery:architecture` first.
- **Setup, not a feature** — if the item is pure environment/repo/framework/build-system setup (no persona completes a journey through it), refuse to write it as a story; point back to `architecture.md`'s Setup section, where it belongs as a Phase-1-gating prerequisite, not a phase deliverable.
- Never overwrite a story whose status is `in-progress` or `done` — supersede it instead, per the protocol below.

## When a ruling invalidates existing stories

A decision that lands mid-flight does not entitle you to rewrite history. What you do
depends on whether work has started, and **nothing is ever deleted** — a story is a record
of what was intended, and deleting it destroys the reason the code looks the way it does.

| Status | What to do |
| :-- | :-- |
| `draft` | Revise in place. No work is lost and nothing referenced it yet. |
| `ready` | Revise in place, and note in the story what changed and which ruling caused it. Someone may have read it. |
| `in-progress` | **Coordinate stopping active work with its owner first; do not terminate it unilaterally.** Mark `superseded`, record what was actually built, and say whether that partial work is kept, reverted, or left for the replacement to absorb. Then write the replacement. |
| `done` | Mark `superseded`. It shipped — the record stands as the explanation for code that exists. Write a new story for the change. |

**Link both directions.** The old story gets `superseded_by: [<new-id>]` and a one-line
reason. The new story gets `supersedes: [<old-id>]`. Without both, the next reader finds a
story describing behaviour the code does not have and cannot tell whether it is stale or
broken.

**Give the reason, not just the link.** "Superseded by p1-15" says nothing. "Superseded by
p1-15: the owner ruled that out of season the estimate is disabled rather than falling back
to a minimum rate" tells a future reader why the design changed, which is the part worth
keeping.

**A superseded story is not a failed story.** It records a decision that was correct given
what was known. Treat the supersession as information about how the understanding moved,
and say so in the sprint review's calibration section — a design that supersedes often is a
design being learned, and that is worth knowing.

Resolve the target phase from `the user's request`, or take the first phase in the roadmap with no stories yet. State which phase you are decomposing before you start.

**Open blocking findings.** Apply the conventions' *Open blocking findings* check to every artifact this phase consumes before going further.

## Run

**0. Decompose once, then choose an available drafting mode.**

Deciding *what the stories are* is one judgement over the whole phase and must happen once,
in sequence: the slice boundaries, the dependency order, what each story owns. That is fast.

**Writing** them is not one judgement — it is N independent ones. Each story is
self-contained by construction, so nothing in story 7 depends on the prose of story 3.
When native delegation is available and authorized, dispatch drafts in parallel, one
reviewer per story, passing the decomposition, slice and shared context. Reviewers
return drafts without writing files; reconcile and write centrally. Otherwise write
sequentially, explicitly naming the single-session mode.

Sequential drafting is the valid fallback when delegation is unavailable or
prohibited. Do not claim a speedup or independent review without observing it.

Then reconcile centrally: interfaces named in one story must match the others, dependency
IDs must resolve, and no two stories may claim the same file for the same change. That
check is cheap and it is the only part that genuinely needs the whole set in hand.

**1. Delivery Manager decides the decomposition.** Use the `delivery-lead` lens.

The governing rule: **the story file is the complete context.** Someone opening one story file — a teammate who missed the planning, or an agent with no memory of it — must have everything needed to finish it. Extract the relevant slices of the PRD and architecture *into* the story. Do not link out. A story requiring three other documents to be read has failed at its one job.

Each story carries: the owner's ask (quoted, with a citation to the actual decision when available), its customer surface (an id from `surface.json`), acceptance criteria written as outcomes the customer sees on that surface (never a tool, endpoint, test, link or ticket), one probe per criterion (what is observed, where, by `test` or `reality-check`), a measurement plan (signal, numeric threshold, where), the shippable unit, user-facing goal, real verified file paths, the interfaces and contracts it must honor, the architecture decisions that apply and why, acceptance criteria traced to `FR-n`, the test approach with the actual command to run tests in this repo, dependencies on other stories, and explicit out-of-scope notes.

**2. Each writer carries the design system into its UI story.** Where `design-system.md` exists, each story touching UI names the **tokens by their real project name**, the component states it must implement (including error and empty), and the accessibility rules that apply. An implementer who cannot find the token reaches for a raw value, and the design system erodes one commit at a time — naming them in the story is what prevents that.

**3. Verify the file paths exist.** The Delivery Manager cites paths; you check them against the repo. A story pointing at a file that does not exist sends the implementer looking for something imaginary.

**4. QA Strategist sets the test approach** per story — the level, the negative and boundary cases, and how it is verified.

**5. Planning readiness check.** For each story, verify falsifiable customer outcomes,
real paths, required sections, declared surface, dependencies and an executable test
approach. Record `ready` only as **planning-ready, manually reviewed**; missing inputs
leave it `draft` with the reason. This preview has no criteria-hash stamp, claim gate,
Beads materialisation or authority to start builders. Changed criteria require renewed
review; preserve the old criteria in the document history.

**6. Write the stories** to `.delivery/stories/<initiative>-<epic>-<nn>-<slug>.md` using `../../templates/story.md`, and update the story index at `.delivery/stories/README.md`.

## Exit criteria

- Within the template's budget, or the overrun declared in the document with its reason — measure prose when computation is available; otherwise report word count unverified

- Every story is a vertical slice delivering observable behavior, or states why it cannot be
- Every acceptance criterion in the target phase is covered by at least one story
- Every story's file paths verified against the repo
- Dependencies between stories are explicit
- Each story is finishable in one focused sitting, or is split

## Writing, then revising

**Budget: 700 words target, 1200 hard cap** (excludes code, YAML and data tables). Compose, measure and revise as *Writing, then revising* in the conventions says.

## Hand off

Report: stories written, how many are `ready` versus `draft`, and what each draft is missing. Flag any acceptance criterion in the phase that no story covers. Next step: `$delivery:sprint` to scope a wave for an implementation runner.

never claim local initialization or canonical persistence from a prepared draft.

Not necessarily the repository root. Resolve before reading or writing any artifact:

1. **Reuse.** Reuse the nearest existing ancestor `.delivery/`. If there is instead a nested component workspace, select that component explicitly; never create a second one beside it. The helper refuses ambiguity instead of picking a sibling.
2. **Explicit override.** Otherwise honor a delivery-root path stated in the nearest `AGENTS.md`.
3. **Ask, don't guess.** Otherwise, if this repository holds more than one independently-releasable component (multiple `package.json`/`plugin.json`/`pyproject.toml`, workspace members, or similar) stop and ask which component this work belongs to. 4. **Default.** Otherwise, use `.delivery/` at the repository root.

## Which initiative

Every artifact below lives under `.delivery/initiatives/<slug>/`, never directly under
`.delivery/` — this is what lets independent initiatives (epics, sprints, parallel
workstreams) be planned in parallel branches without colliding on the same shared file
(`ADR-004`; the incident that motivated it: two initiatives independently continued the same
`S-n`/`FR-n` sequence in one shared `prd.md`, discovered only at merge). Resolve which
initiative before reading or writing any artifact:

1. **Explicit signal.** The user names an initiative, or one is already established for this

2. **Exactly one exists.** If `.delivery/initiatives/` has exactly one subdirectory, use it

   reuses an existing initiative's problem framing instead of running its own — state which,
   don't leave it implicit.

`.delivery/personas/`, `.delivery/interviews/`, `.delivery/simulations/`,
`.delivery/decisions/ADR-NNN-*.md`. This preview has no invocation ledger.
`.delivery/stories/`, `.delivery/reviews/`, `.delivery/sprints/` stay flat but are prefixed
by initiative slug, matching `stories/<slug>-NN-<name>.md`'s existing convention.

## Open blocking findings

Read `.delivery/reviews/`. If any finding against an artifact
this phase consumes has status `open` and severity `blocking`, **stop and report them** — do

building on it means every downstream artifact inherits a known, documented defect with no
resolution on record.

Resolving means the finding is marked `fixed`, or `rejected` with the reason recorded. The
user may still choose to proceed over an open finding — that is their call, not a default.
Ask, and record what they chose.

## Language

Read `.delivery/glossary.md` first and use its terms exactly. If it does not exist, create
it as *Keeping the glossary* below says — or, for a small effort, collect terms as you go and
propose the file at the end. Do not coin synonyms for concepts it already names.

Any term you need that is missing gets **proposed explicitly**, with a definition in the
business's vocabulary and a concrete referent. Any term carrying two meanings gets raised as
a defect, not resolved silently.

**Questions go out in the vocabulary of whoever must answer them**, with a worked example in
their world. A question for the business owner written in engineering terms is a blocker
with a name on it, not a question. If a question is really an engineering call, decide it
here rather than routing it to them.

### Keeping the glossary

`.delivery/glossary.md`, one agreed term per concept, written from
`../templates/glossary.md` (budget: 500 words target, 900 hard cap). It is
project-wide and every skill reads it; any skill that coins or meets a new term adds it.
Every document is written by someone fluent in a different dialect — the analyst's *booking
window* is the architect's *date range* and the owner's *price list* — and the damage shows
at the edges: questions the owner cannot answer, requirements that drift into two concepts,
and a hand-off the runner has to guess at.

1. **Curate, never regenerate.** If the file exists, edit it. Terms are stable: changing a
   definition means saying what it was, what it is now, and which documents were written
   under the old meaning.
2. **Harvest the terms actually in use** — the originator's own words first (they outrank
   everything), then the brief, PRD, personas, architecture, and real identifiers in code
   and data.
3. **Resolve collisions.** Synonyms (several words, one concept): pick one, list the rest as
   *aliases, not to be used*, with the document each came from. Homonyms (one word, several
   concepts): split them and rename at least one.
4. **Let the business word win.** Where domain and code disagree, the domain term is the
   entry and the code identifier is recorded as its implementation name. Do not rename code
   as a side effect.
5. **Define in the owner's words**, plain sentence first, precise one after if needed, and
   **ground each term** in a worked example, a file path or a value from the data.
6. **A term nobody can define crisply** is an unresolved product decision wearing a noun:
   list it as an open question for the originator, never invent a definition.
7. **Sweep for completeness.** Every domain noun in the existing artifacts appears in the
   glossary or is deliberately excluded, and no synonym is left without one canonical term.

**Report what changed** when you hand off: new terms, resolved synonyms, and any term that could
not be defined. Those are product decisions, and they belong to the originator.

During `$delivery:status`, manually compare the active artifacts with the glossary; the inventory helper does not extract domain terms.

## Writing, then revising

The skill states the budget: a word target and a hard cap (both exclude code, YAML and data tables).

**Compose first. Do not try to hit the budget while writing.** Restraint during
composition trades substance for brevity in the wrong order — the findings get thinner
while the scaffolding survives. Write what the artifact needs, then cut what it does not.

**Then measure, do not estimate.** The budget counts **prose only**. Data tables, code
blocks and YAML are excluded, so measure with them stripped:

With local execution, use the helper below. On another surface, use available
computation tools with the same exclusions. If none are available, preserve the
substance and state **word count unverified**; an exact-count exit criterion
remains unverified. Do not invent a count or require a new server for counting.

```sh
python3 <resolved-plugin-root>/scripts/project.py words <artifact-path>
```

The helper strips HTML comments, initial YAML frontmatter, fenced code and
pipe-prefixed table rows before counting prose. Use pipe-prefixed data tables.
Inline code remains prose; this is a Markdown budget convention, not a full parser.

A plain `wc -w` counts the tables and will overstate the total, often by several times.
Measuring the wrong number leads to cutting the wrong thing.

**Rows in a data table can never help you meet the budget, because they are not counted.**
Deleting them is pure loss for zero benefit. The term table, the requirement table, the
findings table, the friction map — these *are* the artifact. If a revision pass is removing
rows, it has misunderstood the rule and should stop.

**If the count exceeds the hard cap, you are not finished.** Make a revision pass over the file and
delete, in this order, until it fits:

1. Preamble, recap, and any sentence describing what the document is about to say
2. **Restatement** — the same fact as prose *and* a table row *and* a summary bullet. Keep the form that carries it best; delete the others. This is almost always the biggest win.
3. Process narration — "I examined X and found Y" becomes Y
4. Hedging — either you know it, or it is labelled an assumption. Both are shorter.
5. Citations past the first for a given claim
6. Examples past the first, unless the next one shows a *different* failure mode

Then re-measure with the same command and confirm.

**Never delete** any row of a data table, findings and their failure scenarios, one citation per claim, grounding
and confidence labels, synthetic-output warnings, open questions, or IDs a later phase
reads. If the artifact cannot fit without losing those, keep them, exceed the cap, and
**write the final count and the reason into the document**. A declared overrun is a
judgement. A silent one is a habit.

---
name: beads
description: Use when working in a repository that uses bd or Beads for durable project task tracking, issue dependencies, blocker management, multi-session handoff, or shared work memory. Trigger when the user asks to find ready work, claim or close tasks, create follow-up work, inspect blockers, recover project context, or choose between local planning and persistent project tracking.
---

# Beads

Use Beads as the shared project task system. Local plans, scratch files, and personal memories are useful, but they are not the durable source of truth for project work.

## First Step

Run:

```bash
bd prime
```

If that prints nothing, check whether the repository has an active Beads workspace:

```bash
bd where
```

## Preferred Route

Use the `bd` CLI when shell access is available. It is the most compact and direct Beads interface.

## Core CLI Workflow

1. Find work:

```bash
bd ready
bd list --status=open
bd list --status=in_progress
```

2. Inspect before editing:

```bash
bd show <id>
```

3. Claim work atomically:

```bash
bd update <id> --claim
```

4. Create durable follow-up work when implementation reveals new tasks:

```bash
bd create "Short title" --description="Why this exists and what needs to be done" --type=task --priority=2
```

5. Close completed work:

```bash
bd close <id> --reason="Completed"
```

## What Belongs In Beads

Use Beads for:

- shared project tasks
- blockers and dependencies
- discovered follow-up work
- work that must survive thread reset, compaction, or handoff
- status that another person or agent should be able to resume

Use agent-local planning tools only for the current turn's execution checklist. Do not treat them as shared project state.

## Rules

- Do not create markdown TODO files as the source of truth when Beads is available.
- Do not use `bd edit`; it opens an interactive editor. Use `bd update` flags instead.
- Prefer `--json` when parsing `bd` output programmatically.
- If hooks are installed, `bd prime` may already be injected. Run it manually when context is missing.
- Do not auto-close or mutate tasks unless the work is actually complete.
